bolivia: Bolivia is a small producer, at about 80,000 bags in the USDA's 2026/27 forecast. Its specialty arabica grows high, around 1,200–2,000 m in the Yungas around Caranavi and Coroico, and is picked from June to October. Importers describe these coffees with fruit, chocolate and floral notes.
brazil: Brazil is the largest producer in the USDA's forecast, at about 71.9 million bags for 2026/27, roughly two-thirds of it arabica. Most of that arabica is dried either in the whole cherry (natural) or with the skin and fruit removed but the sticky mucilage left on (pulped natural), and it grows lower than in Central America, around 800–1,250 m in Sul de Minas and the Cerrado. Importers describe it with chocolate, nut and fruit notes; the harvest runs from about April to September.
burundi: Burundi grows Bourbon-family arabica high in the north, around 1,600–2,150 m in Kayanza and Ngozi, and picks it from March to July. Importers describe its washed coffees with fig, jam, floral and citrus notes, though the washing station and the process change the result. It's a small producer, at about 140,000 bags in the USDA's 2026/27 forecast.
colombia: Colombia harvests somewhere almost all year. In Huila the main crop runs from November to January and the smaller mitaca from May to July, and southern districts can swap the two. It's washed arabica grown around 1,200–2,200 m, from common varieties such as Castillo, Colombia and Caturra; northern coffees are often described as chocolatey and nutty, southern highland ones as citrusy and sweet.
costa_rica: Costa Rica's arabica grows around 700–1,900 m, from the Central and West Valleys to Los Santos (Tarrazú), and is picked from October to March, into April on high farms. Most lots are washed; honey and natural lots are common too, and they tend to bring sweetness and fruit forward. Importers describe its coffees with honey, chocolate and fruit notes.
ecuador: Ecuador harvests somewhere in the country all year, because its highlands, coast and Amazon keep their own calendars. Its mainland specialty arabica grows around 1,200–2,000 m, with Loja and Zamora Chinchipe in the south among its best-known regions, while lowland robusta makes up about 70% of the USDA's 2026/27 forecast of 350,000 bags. Importers describe the specialty arabica as fruity and floral.
el_salvador: El Salvador's coffee grows on volcanic slopes such as Apaneca–Ilamatepec, from about 400 to 2,000 m, and is picked from October to March. Bourbon and Pacas are common, along with the large-beaned Pacamara. Importers describe washed lots with fruit, hazelnut and sweet notes; Pacamara and experimental lots can taste quite different.
ethiopia: Ethiopia grows arabica from many regional landraces rather than a handful of named varieties, mostly between 1,100 and 2,300 m in Sidama, Gedeo (Yirgacheffe), Guji, Jimma and Harar. Washed coffees are often described as floral and citrusy, naturals as fruity and winey. Picking runs from October to January, and Café Imports lists April to June as the usual arrival in the US.
guatemala: Guatemala's washed arabica grows from about 700 m to 1,800 m and above, in Antigua, Huehuetenango, Atitlán and Cobán, and is harvested from November to April. Importers describe it with chocolate, nut, citrus and toffee notes, but the regions differ: Antigua leans to chocolate and nuts, Huehuetenango to fruit and toffee.
honduras: Honduras is the largest producer in Central America in the USDA's 2026/27 forecast, at about 6 million bags. Its arabica grows around 950–1,950 m in regions such as Copán, Marcala and El Paraíso, and is picked from November to April. Importers describe it as sweet, nutty and full-bodied, with a lot of variation between regions and producers.
indonesia: Indonesia mostly grows robusta: about 88% of the USDA's 2026/27 forecast of 11.4 million bags is robusta from the lowlands. The coffee specialty buyers know best is wet-hulled arabica from Sumatra (Aceh and North Sumatra), grown around 1,000–1,500 m, which importers describe as earthy, herbal and savory. Robusta and arabica keep different calendars: Sumatran arabica is picked over a long season, from about October to June, and lowland robusta from about April to July.
kenya: Kenya's washed arabica grows around 1,100–2,300 m in the central highlands, in Nyeri, Kirinyaga, Murang'a and Embu. There are two crops: in Central Kenya the main one runs from October to December and an early crop from May to July (Sucafina); Café Imports gives a wider national window, August to January and April to July. Importers describe its coffees with blackcurrant, citrus and black-tea notes; SL28 and SL34 are its best-known varieties, alongside the newer Ruiru 11 and Batian.
mexico: Mexico's arabica grows around 600–1,800 m, mostly in the south: Chiapas, Veracruz, Oaxaca and Puebla. It's picked from November to March, from October at lower southern sites. Importers describe washed Mexican coffees with chocolate, toffee, citrus and nut notes.
nicaragua: Nicaragua's coffee comes mainly from the northern highlands of Jinotega, Matagalpa and Nueva Segovia, around 600–1,500 m, and is picked from October to March. Importers describe it with dark chocolate, red fruit and tangerine notes. The USDA forecasts about 2.4 million bags for 2026/27.
panama: Panama is a small producer, at about 100,000 bags in the USDA's 2026/27 forecast, best known for Gesha from Boquete, Volcán and Renacimiento in Chiriquí, grown around 1,000–2,200 m. Its conventional coffees are described as sweet, nutty and mild; the floral, tropical profiles are most associated with Gesha. The harvest runs from November to March, later on higher farms.
peru: Peru grows washed arabica along a long stretch of the Andes, around 1,000–2,300 m, from Cajamarca in the north to Cusco in the south, so its harvest spreads from March to September. Importers describe its specialty lots with stone fruit, nut, chocolate, caramel and citrus notes. The USDA forecasts about 4.8 million bags for 2026/27.
rwanda: Rwanda's arabica grows around 1,000–2,100 m, from Lake Kivu and the western highlands to Huye and the east, and Bourbon-family varieties are common. It's picked from March to June, and Café Imports lists September to December as the usual arrival in the US. Importers describe its washed coffees with chocolate, stone fruit, citrus and tea notes.
tanzania: Tanzania grows both species. Washed arabica comes from the slopes of Kilimanjaro and Meru and the southern highlands of Mbeya and Ruvuma, from about 1,000 to 2,500 m; robusta comes from Kagera, and is close to half of the USDA's 2026/27 forecast. The southern arabica harvest runs from May to September and the northern one from July to November. Importers describe the washed arabica as juicy, acidic and complex.
thailand: Thailand's coffee is mostly robusta from the far south, around Chumphon and Ranong, and the USDA counts its 2026/27 forecast of about 900,000 bags as robusta. Specialty buyers know its northern arabica, grown around 1,100–1,600 m near Chiang Rai and Chiang Mai and picked from November to February in Chiang Rai and December to March in Chiang Mai, which importers describe with stone fruit, jasmine and dark chocolate notes.
